name: Antonio Vivaldi
why: His first wave, from 1926 to 1933, came mostly in modern orchestral arrangements led by Toscanini, Mengelberg and Bernardino Molinari. The return was led by Guido Cantelli, with 21 of the 42 performances from 1953-54 to 1959-60, and then Leonard Bernstein. It came during the postwar Vivaldi revival.
story: Vivaldi came back with the postwar Vivaldi boom: Bernardino Molinari’s 1942 recording of The Four Seasons, Louis Kaufman’s in 1947, I Musici’s in 1955. At the Philharmonic the return was led by Guido Cantelli, the young Italian of whom Toscanini wrote, “This is the first time in my long career that I have met a young man so gifted.” Cantelli first conducted the orchestra in January 1952. He was killed in a plane crash at Orly in 1956, a week after La Scala named him music director.

name: William Walton
why: Before the gap, John Barbirolli, then the music director, led 11 of his 18 performances, mostly Façade. Walton faded after Barbirolli left. He came back when he conducted his own music at Lewisohn Stadium in August 1963; Josef Krips, Malcolm Sargent and André Kostelanetz kept him on the chart for the next few seasons.
story: Walton’s first run here belonged to John Barbirolli, who gave the world premiere of his second Façade suite with the Philharmonic in 1938. When Barbirolli went home to England, Walton faded too; he once advised “all sensitive composers to die at the age of 37.” He came back in person, conducting his own music at Lewisohn Stadium in August 1963.

name: György Ligeti
why: Before the gap, Pierre Boulez’s Lontano in the 1970s (Boulez led 9 of 21 performances). The return began in the 2006-07 season, months after Ligeti died in June 2006, with Alan Gilbert leading the Violin Concerto. Gilbert later conducted Le Grand Macabre (2010), and Esa-Pekka Salonen brought three works in 2010-11.
story: Most people first heard Ligeti in 2001: A Space Odyssey, where Kubrick used his music “without Ligeti’s knowledge”; Ligeti sued, and they settled out of court. The Philharmonic all but dropped him after Boulez left. He died in June 2006, and the return began that autumn. In 2010 Alan Gilbert staged Le Grand Macabre in his first season as music director, the opera’s first complete performance in New York, and in 2013 he put Ligeti back beside Kubrick in a concert built around 2001.

name: Richard Rodgers
why: A Lewisohn Stadium regular: his show tunes were played there every summer from 1945 to 1964, and he dropped out when the Stadium summers ended. He came back through a new format, Broadway nights in the main season: Barbara Cook singing Rodgers in 2007, then a staged concert of Carousel in 2013.
story: For twenty summers Rodgers belonged to Lewisohn Stadium, the Philharmonic’s summer home from 1922 to 1964. When the orchestra stopped going, Rodgers left its repertoire; the Stadium was torn down in 1973. He came back in 2007, when Barbara Cook celebrated her 80th birthday with the orchestra singing his songs, and in 2013 with a staged Carousel starring Kelli O’Hara and Nathan Gunn, broadcast on PBS.

name: Carl Nielsen
why: One conductor’s project. Alan Gilbert led every Nielsen performance from 2010-11 to 2014-15 while recording all the symphonies and concertos for Dacapo, Denmark’s national label, ahead of Nielsen’s 150th birthday in 2015.
story: The Philharmonic gave Nielsen his international breakthrough: Bernstein’s 1962 recording of the Fifth Symphony. Then the orchestra let him go for 25 years. Alan Gilbert brought him back. He came to love Nielsen in Sweden, “where Danish music is totally standard fare,” and recorded all the symphonies and concertos for Denmark’s Dacapo label in time for Nielsen’s 150th birthday in 2015.
